sections.title: Creating a New Table from an Existing Table

blocks.text: Every statement you have written so far has pointed at KimTay's real tables, and every one of them has been a `SELECT`. A `SELECT` only reads. Module 6 is about statements that change what is stored, and a change you get wrong is not something you can undo by looking away from the screen. So the first skill in this module is not changing data at all. It is making yourself a working copy to change instead.

SQL can build a brand-new table out of the rows a query returns. You write `CREATE TABLE`, the name you want for the new table, the word `AS`, and then an ordinary `SELECT`. Whatever that `SELECT` returns becomes the contents of the new table.
**Start with the data:** this is the complete `ITEM` table that the first statement copies. Inspect the original five rows before `ITEM_COPY` is created.

blocks.caption: Source table: ITEM — the original table before any changes

blocks.text: `ITEM_COPY` now exists and holds all five item rows. It has the same six column names in the same order, because `SELECT *` handed over all six. From this point on you can do anything you like to `ITEM_COPY` and `ITEM` never notices.

blocks.caption: ITEM_COPY immediately after it is created: all six columns, all five rows

blocks.label: Why the price reads 42.5 and not 42.50
blocks.text: The database stores a number, not a piece of formatting. The value 42.50 and the value 42.5 are the same number, so the trailing zero is not printed back to you. That is a display detail, not a change to your data. Formatting money for a report is a separate job from storing it.
Copying only part of a table
The query does not have to be `SELECT *`. Name the columns you want and add a `WHERE` clause, and the new table gets only that slice of the original.

CREATE TABLE HABITAT_ITEM AS
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, ON_HAND, PRICE
FROM ITEM
WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat';

`HABITAT_ITEM` ends up with four columns instead of six and two rows instead of five. The `CATEGORY` column is not in the new table at all, because you did not ask for it, even though the `WHERE` clause used it.

blocks.caption: HABITAT_ITEM after the copy: four columns, two rows

blocks.label: Where the new column names come from
blocks.text: The new table's column names come from the `SELECT` list. If you alias a column with `AS`, the alias becomes the column name in the new table. A computed column always needs an alias, because an expression like `ON_HAND * PRICE` is not a legal column name.

`ITEM_VALUE` has three columns: `ITEM_ID`, `ITEM_NAME`, and `STOCK_VALUE`. Its `STOCK_VALUE` numbers were computed once, when the table was built. They are a snapshot. Change a price in `ITEM` tomorrow and `ITEM_VALUE` will still show yesterday's arithmetic.
What does not come along
This is the part that gets missed, on exams and in real jobs. `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` copies the column names and the rows. It does not copy the rules that were protecting the original table.

items: The primary key. `ITEM_COPY` has an `ITEM_ID` column, but nothing stops two of its rows from both saying `AV07`.
Foreign keys. A copy of `CUSTOMER` will cheerfully hold a `REP_NUM` that matches no rep in `REP`.
`NOT NULL` and `DEFAULT` settings that were declared on the original columns.
Any index that was built on the original table.

blocks.label: The column types come across as families, not as exact declarations
blocks.text: Ask this sandbox for the copy's structure and you will see `ITEM_ID TEXT`, `PRICE NUM`, and `ON_HAND INT`, not the `CHAR(4)`, `DECIMAL(7,2)`, and `SMALLINT` that `ITEM` actually declares. SQLite rebuilds each column with a general type big enough to hold the values it copied. That is fine for a scratch table and one more reason never to promote one into the real database. MySQL and Oracle do keep the original declared types.
You can prove the primary key is gone with one statement. Run this against the copy and it succeeds.

INSERT INTO ITEM_COPY
VALUES ('AV07', 'Second Aviary Starter Cage', 'Habitat', 9, 64.99, 5);

`ITEM_COPY` now has six rows, two of which claim to be item `AV07`. Run the identical statement against `ITEM` instead and the database refuses it with a message about a unique constraint failing on `ITEM.ITEM_ID`. Same statement, same data, different answer, because only one of those two tables still has a primary key.

blocks.label: A copy is a place to make mistakes, not a place to keep data
blocks.text: Because none of the constraints came along, a working copy will accept duplicates, orphans, and blanks that the real table would have caught. That is exactly what makes it a safe scratch pad and exactly what makes it unfit to be promoted into the real database later. Test on the copy, then run your verified statement against the original.
An empty copy of the structure
Sometimes you want the shape of a table without any of its rows, so you have somewhere to collect rows later. Give the query a condition that can never be true and you get exactly that.

CREATE TABLE ITEM_ARCHIVE AS
SELECT *
FROM ITEM
WHERE 1 = 0;

`1 = 0` is false for every row, so no row qualifies and nothing is copied. The column list is still built from `SELECT *`, so `ITEM_ARCHIVE` comes out with six correctly named columns and zero rows. This is a common trick and you will use it again in 6-3, where you need a target table whose columns line up perfectly with the query that fills it.
Cleaning up after yourself
A working table is trash once you are done with it. `DROP TABLE` removes the table and everything in it in one step, and there is no undo.
DROP TABLE ITEM_COPY;

Adding `IF EXISTS` makes the statement safe to run even when the table is not there, which is why the exercises in this module open with it. Without `IF EXISTS`, dropping a table that does not exist is an error, and creating a table that already exists is an error too.
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ITEM_COPY;

blocks.label: Name throwaway tables like throwaways
blocks.text: Use names that announce what they are: `ITEM_COPY`, `CUSTOMER_TEST`, `ITEM_ARCHIVE`. A table named `ITEM2` found in a database six months from now is a mystery nobody wants to solve. A table named `ITEM_COPY` is obviously somebody's scratch paper and can be dropped without a meeting.

blocks.label: Other engines
blocks.text: MySQL and Oracle both support `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT`, and on all three engines the rows come across while the primary key, the foreign keys, and the indexes do not. The engines part company on the smaller details. MySQL and Oracle keep each column's declared data type and carry a `NOT NULL` constraint over to the copy; SQLite keeps neither. So the headline lesson travels everywhere, but do not assume a copy made in Oracle is constrained the same way as a copy made here.

items.title: Copy
items.body: Run `CREATE TABLE ITEM_COPY AS SELECT * FROM ITEM;` so the original is out of the line of fire.

items.title: Confirm
items.body: Run `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ITEM_COPY;` before you touch anything. You should see 5. Knowing the starting count is what lets you notice later that something changed too many rows.

items.title: Work
items.body: Point your `UPDATE`, `INSERT`, and `DELETE` statements at `ITEM_COPY`. Get the statement right there, where being wrong costs nothing.

items.title: Discard
items.body: Run `DROP TABLE ITEM_COPY;` and then run the statement you verified against the real `ITEM` table.

blocks.starter:
-- 1. Build a working copy of ITEM called ITEM_COPY.
-- 2. Insert a second row that reuses the item id AV07.
-- 3. List ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION and ON_HAND from the copy, ordered by id.
-- The DROP line lets you run this whole script again from a clean copy.

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ITEM_COPY;

CREATE TABLE ITEM_COPY AS
SELECT *
FROM ITEM;
blocks.hint: `SELECT *` copies all six columns, so the `INSERT` needs six values in that same order: id, description, category, on hand, price, reorder level. Finish by selecting from `ITEM_COPY`, not from `ITEM`. You should get six rows back, with `AV07` appearing twice.

I can copy only some columns and only some rows by editing the query.
I can explain that the column names and rows are copied but the primary key, foreign keys, `NOT NULL`, defaults, and indexes are not.
I know the copy's column types are rebuilt as general types in this engine, not carried over exactly.
I can build an empty table with the right columns using `WHERE 1 = 0`.
I can drop a working table when I am finished with it, and I know what `IF EXISTS` adds.

sections.title: Changing Existing Data in a Table

blocks.text: Prices go up. A customer pays down a balance. A rep retires and someone else takes over the account. The rows in a table are not carved in stone, and `UPDATE` is the statement that changes what is already there. It does not add rows and it does not remove them. It reaches into rows that already exist and replaces values in them.

An `UPDATE` has three parts. You name the table you are changing. You write a `SET` clause giving each column its new value. You write a `WHERE` clause saying which rows. That third part is optional as far as the database is concerned and mandatory as far as you are concerned, for reasons that will be uncomfortably clear by the end of this section.
Work on a copy. Build one first, then change the price of the nylon leash on the copy.
Exactly one row matched, so exactly one row changed. In `ITEM_COPY` the leash now costs 12.49. In `ITEM` it still costs 11.99, because you never touched `ITEM`.
Changing several columns at once
Separate the assignments with commas. One `UPDATE` statement, one pass over the table, as many columns as you need.

UPDATE ITEM_COPY
SET PRICE = 12.49,
    REORDER_LEVEL = 40
WHERE ITEM_ID = 'DG04';

Notice there is only one `SET`. The word appears once, no matter how many columns follow it. Do not write two separate `UPDATE` statements for two columns of the same row. One statement is less work for the database, and more importantly it cannot leave the row half-changed if something goes wrong between the two.
New values can be computed

The right side of an `=` in a `SET` clause is an expression, not only a typed-in constant. It can even refer to the column's own current value, and when it does, the database uses the value the row had before this statement started running. That is how you raise a whole category of prices without knowing any of them.

Two rows are in the `Habitat` category, so two rows change. `ROUND(value, 2)` rounds the result to two decimal places. It rounds, it does not chop: the raw arithmetic for the aviary cage is 68.2395, so `ROUND` stores 68.24, not the 68.23 you would get by simply cutting the extra digits off. Leave `ROUND` out entirely and the cage is stored as 68.2395, which is not a price anybody can charge.

blocks.caption: The Habitat rows before and after a five percent increase

blocks.text: The WHERE clause can hold a subquery

Anything that is legal in a `SELECT` statement's `WHERE` clause is legal in an `UPDATE` statement's `WHERE` clause, including the subqueries from Module 5. The database works out which rows match, then changes those rows.

CREATE TABLE CUSTOMER_COPY AS
SELECT *
FROM CUSTOMER;

UPDATE CUSTOMER_COPY
SET CREDIT_LIMIT = CREDIT_LIMIT + 1000.00
WHERE REP_NUM IN
      (SELECT REP_NUM
       FROM REP
       WHERE CITY = 'Brookville');

The subquery returns rep 65, the only rep in Brookville. Whiskers & Wags Boutique is the only customer assigned to that rep, so one row changes and its credit limit goes from 6000 to 7000. The other three customers are untouched. You never had to know which rep number Brookville corresponded to; the subquery worked that out.
The forgotten WHERE

Leave the `WHERE` clause off entirely and the statement is still perfectly valid SQL. It means every row in the table. The database does not ask whether you are sure. There is no confirmation prompt, no warning, and no undo.
UPDATE ITEM_COPY SET ON_HAND = 0;

All five items now read zero on hand: the cage, the food, the leash, the filter kit, and the grooming kit. Nothing was misspelled. No error appeared. The inventory counts are simply gone, and the old values are not saved anywhere for you to get back.

blocks.caption: ITEM_COPY after an UPDATE with no WHERE clause

blocks.label: Read the WHERE clause twice before you run it
blocks.text: An `UPDATE` with no `WHERE` changes every row in the table. An `UPDATE` whose `WHERE` names the wrong column changes the wrong rows just as quietly. This is the single most common way working databases get damaged, and it is almost never caused by a hard query. It is caused by a fast one.
The habit that prevents this costs about five seconds. Before you run the `UPDATE`, run the same `FROM` and `WHERE` as a `SELECT` and look at what comes back.

One row comes back: the nylon leash, priced 11.99 with a reorder level of 25. That is what you meant to change, so the `UPDATE` built on the same `WHERE` clause is safe to run. If that `SELECT` had returned five rows when you expected one, you would have found the problem while it was still free to fix.

blocks.label: Rehearse, then commit
blocks.text: Write the `SELECT` first. When it returns exactly the rows you want, turn it into the `UPDATE` by replacing the `SELECT ... FROM` part with `UPDATE ... SET`. The `WHERE` clause is never retyped, and retyping is where typos come from.

blocks.label: Matching nothing is not an error either
blocks.text: If you mean to update `DG04` and you type `DG40`, the statement succeeds and changes zero rows. No message, no complaint. That is safer than the alternative, but it also means that seeing no error is not proof that anything happened. Always look at the table afterward.

items.title: Copy
items.body: Build a working table with `CREATE TABLE ITEM_COPY AS SELECT * FROM ITEM;` so a mistake costs you nothing.

items.title: Rehearse
items.body: Run your `WHERE` clause as a `SELECT` against the copy and count the rows it returns. Is that the number you expected?

items.title: Update the copy
items.body: Change `SELECT ... FROM` to `UPDATE ... SET`, leaving the `WHERE` clause exactly as it was.

items.title: Verify
items.body: Select the changed rows back out and read the new values with your own eyes. Also check that a row you did not intend to change still looks right.

items.title: Run it for real
items.body: Only now, point the verified statement at the real table.

blocks.starter:
-- The Nylon Dog Leash 6ft (DG04) is being repriced to 12.49
-- and its reorder level raised to 40. Do BOTH in one UPDATE.
-- Work on a copy, then list the whole copy so you can check your work.
-- The DROP line means you can rerun this script for a fresh copy.

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ITEM_COPY;

CREATE TABLE ITEM_COPY AS
SELECT *
FROM ITEM;
blocks.hint: The word `SET` appears once. Put a comma between the two assignments, not the word `AND`. If your result shows all five items with a price of 12.49, you left off the `WHERE` clause: run the whole script again from the top, because the `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` line rebuilds the copy from the untouched `ITEM` table.

items: I can write an `UPDATE` with `SET` and `WHERE` that changes one specific row.
I can change several columns in one statement by separating the assignments with commas.
I can compute a new value from the column's current value, and round it to two decimal places.
I know `ROUND` rounds rather than truncates, so 68.2395 becomes 68.24 and not 68.23.
I can use a subquery inside an `UPDATE` statement's `WHERE` clause.
I can explain exactly what an `UPDATE` with no `WHERE` clause does, and why no error appears.
I rehearse the `WHERE` clause as a `SELECT` before I run the `UPDATE`.

sections.title: Adding New Rows to an Existing Table

blocks.text: Module 3 taught you `INSERT INTO ... VALUES`, which adds one row that you type out yourself. That is the right tool when a shipment arrives and somebody hands you the details of a new item on a piece of paper. Nothing in the database knows about that item yet, so somebody has to key it in.

It is the wrong tool when the rows you need are already sitting in the database and there are two hundred of them. Retyping data that the database already has is slow, and every retyped character is a chance to introduce an error that was not there before.
So `INSERT` has a second form. Replace the `VALUES` clause with a `SELECT`, and every row that query returns becomes a row in the target table. One statement, however many rows the query finds.
Building the target first
The table you are inserting into has to exist already. `INSERT` never creates a table. Build it with a plain `CREATE TABLE` and a column list, exactly the way Module 3 showed.

CREATE TABLE PREMIUM_CUSTOMER
    (CUSTOMER_NUM CHAR(4),
     CUSTOMER_NAME CHAR(35),
     BALANCE DECIMAL(9,2),
     CREDIT_LIMIT DECIMAL(9,2));
Now load it. KimTay wants every customer whose credit limit is 7500 or more.

INSERT INTO PREMIUM_CUSTOMER
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CREDIT_LIMIT >= 7500.00;

Two customers qualify, so two rows are added. Look closely at what is not in that statement: no `VALUES`, no parentheses wrapped around the query, and no semicolon between the `INSERT` line and the `SELECT` line. It is one single statement that happens to occupy four lines.
Making the columns line up

The `SELECT` list has to match the target table's columns by count and by position. Names have nothing to do with it. The first value goes into the first column, the second into the second, and so on, no matter what anything is called.
If the counts disagree, the statement fails and nothing at all is inserted. That is the good outcome.

The database rejects that. In this sandbox the message is "table PREMIUM_CUSTOMER has 4 columns but 2 values were supplied". The exact wording differs between engines; the refusal does not. All three of SQLite, MySQL, and Oracle stop you here.

blocks.label: The dangerous case is when the counts agree
blocks.text: If you supply the right number of values in the wrong order, nothing errors. Balances land in the credit limit column and credit limits land in the balance column, and the statement reports success. Naming the target columns explicitly, right after the table name, is what protects you from this.

CREATE TABLE REP_NAME
    (REP_NUM CHAR(2),
     FULL_NAME CHAR(32));

INSERT INTO REP_NAME (REP_NUM, FULL_NAME)
SELECT REP_NUM, FIRST_NAME || ' ' || LAST_NAME
FROM REP
WHERE RATE > 0.05;

`(REP_NUM, FULL_NAME)` after the table name says which columns you are filling and in what order. Richard Hull's rate of 0.07 is the only one above 0.05, so `REP_NAME` gets one row: `35` and `Richard Hull`. The `||` operator glued the first name, a space, and the last name into one value, which shows that the query feeding an `INSERT` can compute values that exist in no column anywhere.

blocks.label: `||` is not portable, `CONCAT()` is closer
blocks.text: `||` means concatenate in this sandbox and in Oracle. MySQL reads `||` as a logical OR unless the server has been specially configured, so the same statement there would produce a number, not a name. Write `CONCAT(FIRST_NAME, ' ', LAST_NAME)` if you want one spelling that works in all three. `CONCAT()` runs here too, and returns the identical `Richard Hull`.

INSERT INTO REP_NAME (REP_NUM, FULL_NAME)
SELECT REP_NUM, CONCAT(FIRST_NAME, ' ', LAST_NAME)
FROM REP
WHERE RATE > 0.05;
The query can be as complicated as you like
Whatever a `SELECT` can produce, an `INSERT` can store. That includes grouped and aggregated results, which is how summary tables get built.

CREATE TABLE REP_TOTAL
    (REP_NUM CHAR(2),
     CUST_COUNT SMALLINT,
     TOTAL_BALANCE DECIMAL(9,2));

INSERT INTO REP_TOTAL
SELECT REP_NUM, COUNT(*), SUM(BALANCE)
FROM CUSTOMER
GROUP BY REP_NUM;

`GROUP BY REP_NUM` produces one row per rep, so three rows are inserted. Rep 20 carries two customers whose balances add up to 3512.5, because Companion Care Clinic's balance is 0.00 and Access Pet Center's is 3512.50. The other two reps have one customer each.

blocks.label: A summary table is a photograph, not a window
blocks.text: `REP_TOTAL` holds the numbers as they stood the instant the `INSERT` ran. Change a balance in `CUSTOMER` afterward and `REP_TOTAL` does not follow along. If you need numbers that are always current you want a view, which is coming later. If you need a record of what the numbers were on a particular day, a table like this is exactly right.
Combining what you learned in 6-1

Writing out a `CREATE TABLE` column list by hand only to match a table you already have is tedious and easy to get wrong. The `WHERE 1 = 0` trick from 6-1 builds the target for you with columns that already line up perfectly with the source.

CREATE TABLE BUDGET_ITEM AS
SELECT *
FROM ITEM
WHERE 1 = 0;

`BUDGET_ITEM` has ITEM's six columns and no rows. Now both forms of `INSERT` work on it. Use `INSERT ... SELECT` to bulk-load the rows that already exist, and `INSERT ... VALUES` for a brand-new item that is in no table yet. They are not competing techniques; most real loading jobs use both.
Running the same load twice
`INSERT` adds. That is all it does. It does not check whether a matching row is already sitting there, and it does not synchronize the target with the source.

blocks.label: A second run doubles your rows
blocks.text: Run the `PREMIUM_CUSTOMER` load once and you have two rows. Run the identical statement again and you have four, two of which are exact duplicates. Nothing complains, because that table has no primary key to complain with. Before you re-run a load, either check what is already in the target or empty it first.

cards.title: INSERT ... VALUES
cards.body: One row per statement, typed out by hand. Use it when the data is new to the database and has to come in from outside: a shipment, a phone call, a paper form. The row count is small and known.

cards.title: INSERT ... SELECT
cards.body: As many rows as the query returns, in one statement. Use it when the data is already in the database and you are copying, filtering, or summarizing it. The row count depends on the data, and can be zero.

blocks.starter:
-- KimTay wants a BUDGET_ITEM table holding every item under $20,
-- plus one brand-new item that is not in ITEM yet:
--   TY01, Rope Chew Toy, Accessory, 60 on hand, 7.25, reorder at 20.
-- Build the empty table first, then use BOTH forms of INSERT.
-- The DROP line lets you rerun this script from scratch.

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS BUDGET_ITEM;

CREATE TABLE BUDGET_ITEM AS
SELECT *
FROM ITEM
WHERE 1 = 0;
blocks.hint: `BUDGET_ITEM` has all six of ITEM's columns, so both inserts have to supply six values. The bulk load uses `SELECT` and no `VALUES` keyword; the single new item uses `VALUES` and no `SELECT`. You should finish with three rows: DG04, GR15, and TY01.

items: I can write `INSERT INTO ... SELECT` to load many rows from a query in one statement.
I can say when `INSERT ... VALUES` is the better choice and when `INSERT ... SELECT` is.
I know the target table must already exist, and I can build it with `CREATE TABLE` or with `WHERE 1 = 0`.
I can explain why the column count and order matter more than the column names.
I name the target columns explicitly to keep values from landing in the wrong place.
I know `||` joins strings here and in Oracle, and that MySQL needs `CONCAT()`.
I know that re-running an `INSERT ... SELECT` adds the rows a second time.

questions.stem: A clerk runs `CREATE TABLE ITEM_COPY AS SELECT * FROM ITEM;` and then tries to insert a row into `ITEM_COPY` using the item id `AV07`, which the Aviary Starter Cage already uses. What does the database do?
options: The copy rejects it, because CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT brings the primary key over along with the rows
The copy rejects it, because SQL never permits two rows to share a value in any column
The copy accepts it, because the statement copied the column names and rows but not the primary key
The copy accepts it only after you first run an ALTER TABLE statement to drop the primary key
optionNotes: This is the central misconception of the section. The column names and the rows come across; keys, foreign keys, defaults, and indexes do not.
Duplicate values are perfectly normal in most columns. It is the primary key constraint, not SQL itself, that forbids them in ITEM.
Correct. ITEM_COPY has an ITEM_ID column but no constraint on it, so a second AV07 row goes right in.
There is no key on the copy to drop, so this step would fail and is not needed in the first place.
questions.takeaway: CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT copies data and column names, never the constraints that were protecting the original.

questions.scenarioTitle: An empty shell for the item archive
questions.stem: The warehouse manager wants a table with ITEM's exact column layout but no data in it yet, and runs `CREATE TABLE ITEM_ARCHIVE AS SELECT * FROM ITEM WHERE 1 = 0;`. What is created?
options: A table with the same six column names as ITEM and no rows in it at all
A table holding all five ITEM rows, because the condition is applied after the copy is made
An error message, because CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT requires the query to return at least one row
A table with one row whose columns are all set to zero, matching the condition 1 = 0
optionNotes: Correct. The condition is false for every row so nothing is copied, but the column list still comes from SELECT *.
The WHERE clause filters rows as the query runs, before anything is written to the new table.
A query returning zero rows is a legitimate query, and the engine builds the table from its column list regardless.
The condition 1 = 0 is a test the database evaluates, not a template for a row of data.
questions.takeaway: A condition that is never true gives you a table's structure with none of its rows, which is exactly what you want as a target for a later load.

questions.scenarioTitle: Monday morning at the KimTay warehouse
questions.stem: Meaning to zero the on-hand count for the grooming kit only, someone runs `UPDATE ITEM_COPY SET ON_HAND = 0;` against a copy holding all five items. What is the result?
options: The statement fails, because SQL requires a WHERE clause on every UPDATE statement
All five rows are set to zero on hand, and the statement reports no error at all
Only the grooming kit changes, because the database infers the row from the most recent SELECT
The database prompts for confirmation before changing more than one row in a single statement
optionNotes: The WHERE clause is optional to the parser. Omitting it is valid SQL that means every row.
Correct. No WHERE means every row, and a successful statement produces no warning of any kind.
The database has no memory of your previous queries. Each statement stands entirely on its own.
There is no confirmation step. This is exactly why the damage is usually discovered hours later.
questions.takeaway: An UPDATE with no WHERE clause changes every row in the table and tells you nothing about it.

questions.stem: The bookkeeper needs to set customer 1420's balance to 0.00 and its credit limit to 8000.00 in a single UPDATE on `CUSTOMER_COPY`. Which SET clause is written correctly?
options: SET BALANCE = 0.00 AND CREDIT_LIMIT = 8000.00, joining the two assignments with the keyword AND
SET BALANCE = 0.00; SET CREDIT_LIMIT = 8000.00, ending each assignment with its own semicolon
SET BALANCE = 0.00 SET CREDIT_LIMIT = 8000.00, repeating the SET keyword before each column
SET BALANCE = 0.00, CREDIT_LIMIT = 8000.00, separating the two assignments with a comma
optionNotes: AND is a logical operator for conditions in a WHERE clause, not a separator for assignments in a SET clause.
A semicolon ends a whole statement, so this would chop one UPDATE into fragments the database cannot parse.
The word SET appears exactly once in an UPDATE statement no matter how many columns are being changed.
Correct. One SET, then a comma-separated list of column-equals-value assignments.
questions.takeaway: Write SET once and separate multiple column assignments with commas, so the whole row changes in one pass.

questions.stem: On a copy of ITEM, someone runs `UPDATE ITEM_COPY SET PRICE = ROUND(PRICE * 1.05, 2) WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat';`. The Aviary Starter Cage starts at 64.99 and the raw arithmetic gives 68.2395. What is stored?
options: 68.23, because ROUND removes any digits past the second decimal place
68.24, because ROUND rounds to two decimal places rather than chopping the extra digits off
68.2395, because ROUND only affects how the value is displayed, not how it is stored
64.99, because a column cannot be updated using its own current value in the expression
optionNotes: That is what truncating would give. ROUND looks at the digits it is dropping and adjusts the last kept digit accordingly.
Correct. The dropped digits are 95, so the second decimal place rounds up from 3 to 4 and 68.24 is stored.
ROUND produces a new value, and the UPDATE stores that value. Display formatting is a separate concern entirely.
Referring to a column's own current value is normal and is exactly how percentage increases are written.
questions.takeaway: ROUND rounds rather than truncates, so verify which one your prices actually need before you commit the change.

questions.stem: A clerk means to reprice item DG04 but types `WHERE ITEM_ID = 'DG40'` instead. What does the database report back?
options: Nothing changes and no error appears, because the WHERE clause simply matched zero rows
An error stating that item DG40 could not be found in the ITEM_COPY table
Every row is updated, because a WHERE clause that matches nothing is treated as no WHERE clause
The nearest matching row, DG04, is updated, because the database corrects small typos in string literals
optionNotes: Correct. Zero matching rows is a normal outcome, so the statement succeeds and quietly does nothing.
Not finding rows is not an error condition. Only a SELECT would show you that nothing matched.
A WHERE clause matching nothing and no WHERE clause at all are opposites, not equivalents.
The database compares values exactly. It has no notion of a near miss or a likely intended value.
questions.takeaway: Seeing no error message is not proof that your UPDATE changed anything, so always read the rows back afterward.

questions.stem: An empty `PREMIUM_CUSTOMER` table already exists, and the bookkeeper needs it filled with every customer whose credit limit is 7500 or more. Which approach does the entire load in one statement, with no values retyped?
options: Run one INSERT ... VALUES statement per qualifying customer after looking each one up by hand
Run CREATE TABLE PREMIUM_CUSTOMER AS SELECT, since the table must be rebuilt in order to receive rows
Run an UPDATE against PREMIUM_CUSTOMER, since the rows already exist somewhere in the database
Run a single INSERT INTO PREMIUM_CUSTOMER followed by a SELECT that returns the qualifying rows

Four rows, because INSERT always adds and PREMIUM_CUSTOMER has no key to reject the duplicates
Two rows plus an error, because a primary key on CUSTOMER_NUM blocks the duplicate values

Correct. Two more copies of the same two rows go in, and nothing in the table is set up to object.

blocks.text: Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` you have written so far took effect the moment you pressed Run. You never told the database to save the change, and you never had a way to take it back. That behavior has a name, it is a setting rather than a law of nature, and this lesson is about turning it off on purpose.
Autocommit: every statement saves itself

Autocommit means the database wraps each statement you send in an invisible save. The statement runs, the change is written to disk, and the database is finished with it. There is no pending state and no undo. Most tools you will meet start this way, because for one quick correction that is exactly what you want.

blocks.label: Autocommit
blocks.text: A session setting. When it is on, the database commits (permanently saves) each statement by itself the instant that statement succeeds. When it is off, your changes pile up unsaved until you say `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`.
Watch it happen. Whiskers & Wags Boutique (customer `1420`) owes KimTay 4820.75. Write the `UPDATE` that takes 200.00 off that balance, then run the whole block. There is no `COMMIT` anywhere in it.

blocks.starter:
-- Autocommit is ON. There is no BEGIN and no COMMIT anywhere below.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE AS BALANCE_BEFORE
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420';

-- Write the UPDATE here: take 200.00 off customer 1420's balance.

SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE AS BALANCE_AFTER
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420';
blocks.hint: Until you write the `UPDATE`, both result sets read 4820.75. With the `UPDATE` in, `BALANCE_BEFORE` comes back 4820.75 and `BALANCE_AFTER` comes back 4620.75. There is no `ROLLBACK` here to protect you, so each Run subtracts another 200.00 — press Reset before you run it a second time.

blocks.text: The balance is now 4620.75, and that number is on disk. If the 200.00 belonged on a different account, no keyword you know so far will bring the old value back. Try the obvious one. Clear the box, type this by itself, and press Run.
ROLLBACK;

blocks.label: The error is the answer
blocks.text: SQLite replies `cannot rollback - no transaction is active`. It is not being difficult. Autocommit ended the transaction the moment your `UPDATE` finished, so there is nothing open left to undo. MySQL is quieter about the same situation, accepting the `ROLLBACK` and changing nothing, but the outcome is identical: the money stays moved.
COMMIT and ROLLBACK

Suspend autocommit and you get two new powers. Your changes become provisional, visible to you and to nobody else, and you decide at the end whether they are real. `COMMIT` says keep everything. `ROLLBACK` says forget everything.

blocks.caption: The three keywords that decide when a change becomes permanent
rows: Opens a transaction and suspends autocommit for the statements that follow
Ends the transaction and keeps every change made inside it
Ends the transaction and discards every change made inside it
Nothing is written, and the rows go back to what they were

blocks.text: Here is the same `UPDATE` as before with `BEGIN;` in front of it and `ROLLBACK;` after it, plus a `SELECT` on each side so you can watch the value move and then move back. Press Reset on the sandbox above, paste this in, and run it.

`INSIDE_TRANSACTION` comes back 4620.75 and `AFTER_ROLLBACK` comes back 4820.75. Between the `BEGIN` and the `ROLLBACK` your session saw the new number and behaved as though it were true. The stored data never moved. That gap between what you can see and what has been saved is the whole idea.
The default is not the same on every engine

blocks.caption: Autocommit by engine, and how you take control of it
rows: Off in SQL*Plus, where the first DML opens a transaction that stays open

blocks.text: This next block is MySQL only, so it is printed as plain text rather than in a sandbox. It switches autocommit off for the session, so the `UPDATE` stays provisional and the `ROLLBACK` really does put the balance back.

Oracle runs the opposite way round, and this line is an Oracle SQL*Plus client command rather than SQL. It asks SQL*Plus to commit after each statement, which is how you make Oracle behave like the others.
SET AUTOCOMMIT ON;

blocks.label: What this sandbox supports
blocks.text: `BEGIN`, `COMMIT`, and `ROLLBACK` all run here. `SET autocommit = 0;` and `SET AUTOCOMMIT ON;` do not exist in SQLite, so the sandbox rejects both — that is why they appear as plain code blocks above. In SQLite the only way to suspend autocommit is to open a transaction with `BEGIN`, which is why every runnable example on this page that needs a transaction starts with that word. The very first sandbox on this page has no `BEGIN` on purpose: it is showing you what autocommit does when you leave it alone.

blocks.label: Do not disconnect with work pending
blocks.text: An open transaction that never reaches `COMMIT` is rolled back when the session ends. On Oracle in particular, closing the window after an afternoon of edits can throw away the whole afternoon. Type `COMMIT;` before you walk away.

items: I can say in one sentence what autocommit does to a single `UPDATE`.
I know why a bare `ROLLBACK;` fails when autocommit is on.
I can open a transaction with `BEGIN;` and end it with `COMMIT;` or `ROLLBACK;`.
I know that MySQL and SQLite default to autocommit on, and Oracle SQL*Plus does not.
I know that leaving a session with work uncommitted discards that work.

blocks.text: A 200.00 delivery charge that belongs to Access Pet Center was posted to Whiskers & Wags Boutique by mistake. Nobody was charged the wrong amount and nobody paid anything. The 200.00 is simply sitting on the wrong account, and moving it takes two statements: take 200.00 off customer `1420` and put 200.00 onto customer `1120`.

Run only the first of those two and KimTay's books are wrong in a way no error message will report. Whiskers & Wags stops owing 200.00 that was never theirs, which is correct, but Access Pet Center is never charged the 200.00 that is theirs, so the money has left the ledger entirely. The two statements are not two jobs. They are one job typed on two lines.

blocks.label: Transaction
blocks.text: A group of statements the database treats as a single unit of work. Either every statement in the group takes effect, or none of them does. Nothing in between is ever stored.

blocks.caption: The correction, and the total that must not move

blocks.text: That last row is the test. A correction that moves a charge between two accounts must leave the total untouched. If the total changes, the correction is broken, and checking it is something you can do in SQL before you save anything.

cards.title: Two statements, autocommit on
cards.body: The first `UPDATE` is saved the instant it succeeds. For however long it takes you to type the second one, the total owed reads 9333.25 and KimTay's books are short 200.00. If your session dies in that gap, nothing brings that 200.00 back.

cards.title: Two statements, one transaction
cards.body: Nothing is saved until you type `COMMIT`. Other sessions keep reading 9533.25 the entire time. When the commit lands, both balances change together, and there is no instant at which the books are wrong.

blocks.text: The shape of every transaction you will ever write

items.title: Open it
items.body: `BEGIN;` suspends autocommit. From here on your changes are provisional and belong to you alone.

items.title: Do all of the work
items.body: Run every statement the job needs. Two, ten, it does not matter. What matters is that they all sit inside the same transaction.

items.title: Check before you save
items.body: Run a `SELECT` that proves the job is right. A total, a count, a look at the rows you touched. This is the step most people skip and the reason `ROLLBACK` exists.

items.title: Decide
items.body: `COMMIT;` if the check passed. `ROLLBACK;` if anything looks wrong. Either keyword closes the transaction and hands autocommit back.

blocks.text: Write the two `UPDATE` statements that move the 200.00, and leave the totals and the `COMMIT` where they are. `TOTAL_OWED_INSIDE` should come back 9533.25, exactly matching `TOTAL_OWED_BEFORE`.

blocks.hint: Both totals read 9533.25, and the final list shows 1120 at 3712.5 and 1420 at 4620.75. SQLite drops trailing zeros when it displays a number, so 3712.50 appears as 3712.5. This script ends in `COMMIT`, so press Reset before running it again or you will move another 200.00.

blocks.text: Half a transaction is worse than no transaction

Here is the failure that catches people out. The second `UPDATE` names customer `9999`, who does not exist. SQL matches no rows, changes nothing, and reports no error at all. Reset the sandbox, paste this in, and run it.

blocks.label: No error does not mean no problem
blocks.text: The first total reads 9333.25. Two hundred dollars have vanished from KimTay's books and nothing on your screen said so. The check `SELECT` caught it, the `ROLLBACK` undid it, and the second total reads 9533.25 again. A statement that matches zero rows is a successful statement, which is why step 3 of a transaction is never optional.
Why the rules have a name
Database people describe a well-behaved transaction with four words, usually shortened to ACID. You do not need to memorize the theory to pass this course, but you have already seen all four at work.

items: Atomicity: all of the statements take effect or none of them do, which is why the half-finished correction above could never reach disk.
Consistency: the database moves from one valid state to another valid state, so the total owed is 9533.25 before and 9533.25 after.
Isolation: your uncommitted changes are yours alone, and other sessions keep reading the old values until you commit.
Durability: once `COMMIT` returns, the change survives a power cut, a crash, or someone tripping over the cable.

blocks.text: Opening a transaction on other engines

The idea is identical everywhere. Only the opening word changes. This version is MySQL, where `START TRANSACTION` is the usual spelling and works even when autocommit is on. SQLite does not accept `START TRANSACTION`, so this is a plain code block rather than a sandbox.

blocks.label: DDL can commit behind your back
blocks.text: On MySQL and Oracle, a data definition statement such as `CREATE TABLE` or `ALTER TABLE` forces an implicit commit before and after itself. Slip an `ALTER TABLE` into the middle of a transaction on those engines and every pending change is saved whether you meant it or not, and a later `ROLLBACK` has nothing left to undo.

SQLite, and therefore this sandbox, does not behave that way. Data definition is transactional here, so you can create a table and then take it back. The check below reads `sqlite_master`, the internal catalog where SQLite keeps one row for every table, index, and view in the database; MySQL answers the same question from `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES`, which SQLite does not have. Paste this into the sandbox above and watch the count go from 1 to 0.

items: I can explain why moving a charge between two accounts is one job, not two.
I open with `BEGIN;`, do all the work, prove it with a `SELECT`, then decide.
I know a statement that matches zero rows reports success, not an error.
I can name a check that would catch a half-finished correction, such as `SUM(BALANCE)`.
I know that `ALTER TABLE` commits implicitly on MySQL and Oracle but not in this sandbox.

blocks.text: `UPDATE` and `DELETE` are the two statements that can destroy work you cannot get back. `INSERT` adds something new, and if it is wrong you delete it. `UPDATE` overwrites a value that is now gone, and `DELETE` removes a row that is now gone. Inside a transaction both become reversible, and this lesson is about building that habit before you need it.
Count the rows before you change them

Both statements act on whatever the `WHERE` clause matches. So find out what it matches first, with a `SELECT` that carries the identical `WHERE`. Companion Care Clinic (customer `1310`) is having its credit limit raised from 10000.00 to 12000.00, and exactly one row should move. Every statement below runs as written in this course's sandbox.

`ROWS_I_AM_ABOUT_TO_CHANGE` comes back 1. That is the number you expected, so the `UPDATE` is safe to run and the `COMMIT` is safe to type. Had it come back 4, you would have known the `WHERE` was wrong before a single value changed. This script does commit, so press Reset afterwards to put the credit limit back to 10000.00.
The WHERE you forgot to type

A missing `WHERE` is not a syntax error. `UPDATE ITEM SET PRICE = ROUND(PRICE * 1.10, 2);` is a perfectly legal statement that raises the price of every product KimTay sells. The engine will not ask whether you meant it. It will report five rows affected and move on.

So make the mistake here, where it costs nothing. The ten percent increase was meant for the two Habitat items, `AV07` and `FT88`, and nothing else. Run the block below top to bottom: it makes the mistake, shows you the damage, and takes it back. Then it leaves you a second transaction to write the version that has the `WHERE` clause on it.

blocks.hint: Four result sets come back every time. Before you write anything they read: the real prices; then 71.49, 46.75, 13.19, 30.53 and 16.78; then the real prices again, because your `UPDATE` is still missing; then the real prices once more. With `WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat'` in place, the third set reads AV07 71.49 and FT88 30.53 while CF21 42.5, DG04 11.99 and GR15 15.25 stay exactly where they were. SQLite drops trailing zeros when it displays a number, so 42.50 appears as 42.5. Both transactions end in `ROLLBACK`, so you can run this as many times as you like without changing anything.

blocks.text: Four result sets come back. The first and the last are identical, and the second one is the damage. Both `UPDATE` statements really did run against the rows: what the `BEGIN` held back was the saving, not the running, and each `ROLLBACK` threw the pending version away before it could reach disk.
The same drill works on `DELETE`, and this one is written out for you. Press Reset, paste it in, and run it.
`LINES_LEFT` reads 0 and `LINES_BACK` reads 6. One statement with no `WHERE` emptied the table, and one word put all six invoice lines back.
6-6a Executing a rollback

`ROLLBACK` is one word with no options and no arguments. It ends the open transaction and returns every row that transaction touched to the value it held at `BEGIN`. It cannot roll back part of the work, and it cannot be aimed at one statement.

items.title: Stop typing
items.body: The transaction is still open, so nothing is on disk yet. Do not try to repair the damage with more `UPDATE` statements while you are still inside it.

items.title: Look at what actually happened
items.body: Run a `SELECT` or a `COUNT(*)`. Knowing whether five rows moved or one row moved decides everything that follows.

items.title: Type ROLLBACK;
items.body: Every change since `BEGIN` disappears at once, and the transaction closes. Autocommit is back in force for the next statement you run.

items.title: Verify, then start over
items.body: Run the same `SELECT` again and confirm the old values are back. Now rewrite the statement with the `WHERE` clause it needed.

blocks.label: ROLLBACK reaches back to the last COMMIT and no further
blocks.text: It is not an undo history. If you commit and then discover the mistake, `ROLLBACK` has nothing to work with. In this sandbox a `ROLLBACK` typed after a `COMMIT` fails with `cannot rollback - no transaction is active`, which is the same message you get from typing it under autocommit.

Run that one and the only thing on your screen is the error, but the `COMMIT` above it was real: customer 1420 is now sitting at a balance of 0 and no keyword will change that. Press Reset before you carry on.

blocks.caption: Which keyword ends the transaction, and when
rows: The rows and totals are exactly what you expected
Written to disk, visible to every session, permanent
More rows changed than you meant to change
Discarded completely, and the rows return to their old values
A statement matched zero rows and left the job half done
Discarded, so no half-finished state is ever stored
Still pending, still private to you, still reversible

blocks.text: The same protection covers deletes. Companion Care Clinic is the only KimTay customer with no invoice, so somebody might reasonably decide the record is dead and remove it. Inside a transaction that decision is reversible.
The count reads 3, then 4. Companion Care Clinic is back, with its address, its balance of 0.00, its credit limit of 10000.00, and its rep. A committed delete would have taken all of that with it.

blocks.label: The habit worth carrying to your first job
blocks.text: Type `BEGIN;` before any `UPDATE` or `DELETE` that touches production data. Run the `SELECT` that proves you were right. Then, and only then, type `COMMIT;`. It costs you two extra lines and it has saved a great many careers.

items: I run a `SELECT` with the same `WHERE` before I run an `UPDATE` or a `DELETE`.
I know a missing `WHERE` is legal SQL that quietly changes every row.
I can update a value, check it, roll back, and confirm the original is restored.
I know `ROLLBACK` undoes the whole transaction and cannot undo one statement.
I know `COMMIT` is the point of no return, and recovery after it means a backup.

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: autocommit, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK

questions.stem: A clerk at KimTay opens a fresh session with autocommit on and runs `UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = BALANCE - 200.00 WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420';`. A second later she realizes the 200.00 belonged on another account and immediately types `ROLLBACK;`. What is the balance for customer 1420 afterward?
options: It returns to 4820.75, because ROLLBACK always reverses the statement that ran before it
It returns to 4820.75, but only if the clerk runs COMMIT immediately afterward
It stays at 4620.75, because autocommit already saved that change permanently
The whole CUSTOMER table returns to the values it held when the session opened
optionNotes: ROLLBACK acts on an open transaction, and autocommit closed this one the instant the UPDATE succeeded.
COMMIT saves pending changes and never restores old ones, and there is no open transaction here for either keyword.
Correct: with autocommit on, the UPDATE was a complete transaction by itself and was written the moment it finished.
No engine keeps a session-long snapshot to fall back on, since rollback reaches to the last COMMIT rather than to login.
questions.takeaway: With autocommit on, every statement is its own committed transaction, so there is nothing left for ROLLBACK to undo.

questions.stem: The administrator turns autocommit off, runs three `UPDATE` statements against `CUSTOMER`, then leaves for lunch without typing anything else. A coworker in a different session runs `SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER;`. What does the coworker see?
options: The original balances, because uncommitted changes stay private to the session that made them
The three updated balances, because all three statements already succeeded without any error
An error message, because the CUSTOMER table is locked until the administrator returns
Two updated balances and one original balance, because rows commit one at a time
optionNotes: Correct: isolation means pending work belongs to its own session, and everyone else keeps reading the last committed values.
Succeeding and committing are different events, and only the second one makes a change visible to other sessions.
Row locks can make another writer wait, but a plain SELECT reads the last committed values instead of failing.
Rows inside one transaction commit together or not at all, so a partial mixture is never what another session reads.
questions.takeaway: Until COMMIT runs, your changes exist only in your own session, no matter how many statements have succeeded.

questions.stem: A student writes a correction script for customer 1225 that has to behave identically on this course sandbox (SQLite), on MySQL at work, and on Oracle in the campus lab. Which statement about autocommit defaults is accurate?
options: All three engines commit every statement automatically, so the script never needs a COMMIT
None of the three commits anything until the session ends, so the script never needs a COMMIT
Oracle and MySQL commit automatically, while SQLite holds every change until the file is closed
SQLite and MySQL default to autocommit, while Oracle SQL*Plus keeps the transaction open until you commit
optionNotes: Oracle SQL*Plus does not commit for you, and disconnecting without a COMMIT discards the work.
SQLite and MySQL both write each standalone statement immediately unless you open a transaction first.
This reverses the real defaults, since SQLite behaves like MySQL here rather than the other way around.
Correct: writing an explicit BEGIN and COMMIT is what makes one script behave the same on all three engines.
questions.takeaway: Never rely on an engine's autocommit default; state your transaction boundaries and the script travels safely.

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: transactions as one unit of work

questions.stem: Inside an open transaction the bookkeeper runs `UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = BALANCE - 200.00 WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420';` and then `UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = BALANCE + 200.00 WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '9999';`. No error appears, but `SELECT SUM(BALANCE) FROM CUSTOMER;` now returns 9333.25 instead of 9533.25. What should happen next?
options: COMMIT the work, since neither statement reported an error back to the bookkeeper
ROLLBACK, because customer 9999 does not exist and 200.00 has gone missing from the total
Run the second UPDATE again with the same customer number until the total corrects itself
COMMIT first, then write a new UPDATE that puts the 200.00 back onto customer 1420
optionNotes: A statement matching no rows is not an error, so a clean run is no proof that the work is correct.
Correct: the transaction is half finished, and ROLLBACK is the one command that returns the books to a consistent state.
Repeating a statement whose WHERE matches nothing changes nothing, because the customer number itself is wrong.
Committing writes the broken total to disk first, and the follow-up fix can fail just as easily as the original did.
questions.takeaway: When the check SELECT shows the job is half done, roll the whole thing back rather than committing and patching.

questions.stem: Power fails in the middle of a transaction that had already run two `UPDATE` statements against `CUSTOMER` but had not yet reached `COMMIT`. When the server comes back up, what is in the table?
options: Both updates, because the two statements had already executed without reporting an error
Only the first update, because it had more time to reach the disk than the second one did
An empty CUSTOMER table, because the crash discarded every row the transaction had touched
Exactly what the table held before BEGIN, because the engine rolls back any transaction that never committed
optionNotes: Executing is not committing, so until COMMIT the changes live in a workspace the crash recovery throws away.
Atomicity means all or nothing, and the engine will never keep one half of a transaction over the other half.
Recovery restores all committed data, so rows the transaction never touched are still exactly where they were.
Correct: durability protects committed transactions, and anything still open at the crash is undone on restart.
questions.takeaway: A crash cannot leave you with half a transaction, because recovery finishes the job by rolling the whole thing back.

questions.stem: Working in MySQL, an analyst types `START TRANSACTION;`, then `UPDATE CUSTOMER SET CREDIT_LIMIT = 12000.00 WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';`, then `ALTER TABLE CUSTOMER ADD COLUMN LAST_REVIEW DATE;`, then `ROLLBACK;`. What is the state of the table?
options: The new column stays and the credit limit stays 12000.00, because the ALTER committed everything pending
Both the column and the credit limit change are undone, because ROLLBACK reverses everything after START TRANSACTION
The credit limit change stays and the new column is dropped, because data definition is never permanent
MySQL rejects the ALTER outright, because data definition is not allowed inside an open transaction
optionNotes: Correct: MySQL and Oracle force an implicit commit around DDL, so the pending 12000.00 was saved before ROLLBACK ran.
That is how the SQLite sandbox behaves, but MySQL and Oracle commit around a data definition statement instead.
Data definition is as permanent as any committed change, and in MySQL it is harder to undo than a plain UPDATE.
The statement is accepted and runs normally; the surprise is what it quietly does to the transaction around it.
questions.takeaway: On MySQL and Oracle, keep data definition statements out of a transaction, because they commit whatever is pending.

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: changing rows, deleting rows, and undoing both

questions.stem: A ten percent increase was meant to hit the two Habitat items only, but the warehouse manager runs `UPDATE ITEM SET PRICE = ROUND(PRICE * 1.10, 2);` inside an open transaction and sees five rows affected. What is the fastest correct recovery?
options: Run `UPDATE ITEM SET PRICE = ROUND(PRICE / 1.10, 2);` to divide every price back down again
Run `DELETE FROM ITEM;` and reload all five rows from the original setup script
COMMIT the change, then correct the three wrong prices one row at a time
Run `ROLLBACK;`, which restores all five original prices and closes the transaction
optionNotes: Dividing everything back also cancels the two Habitat increases that were correct, and rounding is not guaranteed to reverse itself cleanly, so the job still has to be redone.
Deleting and reloading throws away any other work in the transaction and leaves every INVOICE_LINE pointing at rows that no longer exist.
Committing makes the mistake permanent and turns a one-word fix into three hand-typed corrections.
Correct: the transaction is still open, so ROLLBACK discards all five changes at once and puts the prices back.
questions.takeaway: While the transaction is open, ROLLBACK is always cheaper and safer than trying to compute your way back.

questions.stem: A StayWell clerk opens a transaction, deletes a lease row, types `COMMIT;`, and only then learns from the property manager that the lease should have stayed. Can a `ROLLBACK` bring the row back?
options: Yes, because ROLLBACK reverses the most recent statement no matter when that statement ran
No, because ROLLBACK reaches back only as far as the last COMMIT, which has already happened
Yes, but only if no other session has written to the LEASE table since the commit
No, and the reason is that DELETE is a data definition statement that can never be undone
optionNotes: ROLLBACK works on the open transaction, and COMMIT closed it, so a bare ROLLBACK now has nothing to undo.
Correct: COMMIT is the point of no return, so recovery here means restoring a backup or reinserting the row by hand.
Other sessions are irrelevant, because the commit by itself put the change beyond the reach of ROLLBACK.
DELETE is a data manipulation statement and is very much undoable, but only before the transaction commits.
questions.takeaway: COMMIT is the boundary: everything after it is a data recovery problem rather than a SQL problem.

questions.stem: `INVOICE_LINE` holds six rows. A clerk runs `BEGIN;`, then `DELETE FROM INVOICE_LINE WHERE INVOICE_NUM = '50711';`, then `ROLLBACK;`, then `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM INVOICE_LINE;`. What number comes back?
options: 4, because the two deleted rows are gone and ROLLBACK affects only UPDATE statements
0, because ROLLBACK discards the whole table along with the rows that were deleted
6, because ROLLBACK put the two deleted lines back before the count ever ran
2, because the count reports the rows ROLLBACK restored rather than the rows in the table
optionNotes: ROLLBACK undoes every data change made in the transaction, deletes very much included, not only updates.
ROLLBACK returns the table to its state at BEGIN, and it never empties a table that had rows in it.
Correct: invoice 50711 has two lines, CF21 and GR15, both come back, and the table is whole again at six rows.
COUNT(*) always reports what is in the table at the moment it runs, not what a rollback happened to touch.
questions.takeaway: A rolled-back DELETE leaves the table exactly as it was at BEGIN, so the count is the original six.

matchers.heading: Match-up: committed, rolled back, or still open?
matchers.prompt: Each card is a short sequence run against KimTay in one session. Click a card, then click the state the data is in when the sequence finishes. Ask one question of each: has a COMMIT run, has a ROLLBACK run, or is the transaction still sitting there waiting for you to decide?

zones.label: Saved permanently
zones.hint: written to disk, visible to everyone

zones.label: Undone completely
zones.hint: rows back to their old values

cards.text: `UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = BALANCE - 200.00 WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420';` run on its own with autocommit on
cards.why: With autocommit on the statement is its own complete transaction and is written the instant it succeeds.

cards.text: `BEGIN;` then two `UPDATE` statements that move a 200.00 charge from customer 1420 to customer 1120, then `COMMIT;`
cards.why: COMMIT ends the transaction and writes both balance changes to disk together.

cards.text: `BEGIN;` then `UPDATE ITEM SET PRICE = ROUND(PRICE * 1.10, 2);` then `ROLLBACK;`
cards.why: ROLLBACK discards every change since BEGIN, so all five prices return to 64.99, 42.5, 11.99, 27.75 and 15.25 (SQLite displays 42.50 as 42.5).

cards.text: `BEGIN;` then `DELETE FROM INVOICE_LINE;`, and the session is closed without typing anything else
cards.why: An open transaction is rolled back when the session ends, so all six invoice lines survive.

cards.text: `BEGIN;` then `UPDATE CUSTOMER SET CREDIT_LIMIT = 12000.00 WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';` with nothing typed after it yet
cards.why: No COMMIT and no ROLLBACK has run, so the new credit limit is provisional and visible only to this session.

cards.text: `BEGIN;` then `UPDATE ITEM SET ON_HAND = ON_HAND - 1 WHERE ITEM_ID = 'GR15';` then `SELECT ON_HAND FROM ITEM WHERE ITEM_ID = 'GR15';`
cards.why: The SELECT reads the pending value of 21, but reading is not deciding, so the transaction is still open.

cards.text: `ROLLBACK;` typed by itself right after an autocommitted `UPDATE` to customer 1420
cards.why: Autocommit already closed the transaction, so SQLite answers `cannot rollback - no transaction is active`.

cards.text: `BEGIN;` typed a second time while a transaction opened by the first `BEGIN;` is still open
cards.why: SQLite answers `cannot start a transaction within a transaction`, because transactions do not nest here.
