sections.title: Changing a Value in a Column to Null

blocks.text: Sometimes the honest answer is that nobody knows. Suppose KimTay Pet Supplies takes a new account over the phone and whoever answered never wrote down the street address. The row still belongs in `CUSTOMER`, but one column has nothing trustworthy to put in it. Typing a placeholder like `N/A` or `0` turns a gap in your knowledge into a fact that is not true. SQL has a word for the gap itself: `null`.

Every row that ships with this course is completely filled in, so there is not a single null anywhere in the seed data. That is deliberate. If you want to see how nulls behave, you have to create one, and creating one on purpose is exactly what this section teaches: taking a column that currently holds a value and deliberately emptying it, so the database stops claiming something it cannot back up. At the end of the section you will use `IS NULL` to find the row again.

blocks.label: Null
blocks.text: A null is the absence of a value. It is not a number, not a word, and not a blank space. It means the value is unknown, or that the column does not apply to this particular row. Two nulls are never treated as equal to each other, because you cannot say that two unknowns match.
The statement itself

Setting a column to null is an ordinary `UPDATE`. The only difference is that you assign the keyword `NULL` rather than a literal, and you do not wrap it in quotation marks. `'NULL'` in quotation marks is the four-letter word NULL stored as text, which is a real value and defeats the whole point.

blocks.label: Bring a WHERE clause every time
blocks.text: Leaving off `WHERE` sets the column to null in every row of the table, and there is no undo. Run the matching `SELECT ... WHERE ...` first and confirm you get back exactly the rows you meant to touch.

Look at what that statement changes in the shipped data. Companion Care Clinic, customer `1310`, has a `BALANCE` of `0.00`. That zero is a real, verified number: the clinic owes KimTay nothing. Now suppose the account was just migrated from an older system and nobody can confirm the figure. Zero would be a claim you cannot support. Null is the truth.

blocks.starter:
-- Step 1: how the four customers look right now.
SELECT COUNT(*)       AS customer_count,
       COUNT(BALANCE) AS balances_known,
       AVG(BALANCE)   AS average_balance
FROM CUSTOMER;

-- Step 2: set Companion Care Clinic (1310) to a null balance,
-- then run those same three numbers again and compare.
blocks.solution:
SELECT COUNT(*)       AS customer_count,
       COUNT(BALANCE) AS balances_known,
       AVG(BALANCE)   AS average_balance
FROM CUSTOMER;

UPDATE CUSTOMER
SET BALANCE = NULL
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';

SELECT COUNT(*)       AS customer_count,
       COUNT(BALANCE) AS balances_known,
       AVG(BALANCE)   AS average_balance
FROM CUSTOMER;
blocks.hint: `COUNT(*)` counts rows. `COUNT(BALANCE)` counts only the rows where `BALANCE` holds a value. Watch which of the three numbers moves.

blocks.text: Before the update you get `4`, `4`, and `2383.3125`. After it you get `4`, `3`, and `3177.75`. The row count did not change, because the customer is still there. What changed is that one balance stopped counting. `AVG` divided by three instead of four, so the average jumped by almost eight hundred dollars. That is the whole reason null exists as a separate idea: an unknown balance should not be averaged in as if it were zero.

`SUM(BALANCE)` is the interesting control here. It reads `9533.25` both before and after, because the row you emptied held `0.00` and adding zero to a total changes nothing. The total stayed put while the average moved, and the only thing that moved it was the divisor.

blocks.caption: Zero, an empty string, and null are three different things
rows: The customer owes nothing. A real, verified amount.
A text column holding zero characters. Still a value.
Nobody knows, or the column does not apply here.

blocks.text: The empty string is the one that fools people. In a `CHAR` or `VARCHAR` column, `''` looks blank on screen and looks identical to a null in most result grids, but the database considers it a stored value. Build your own two-row table and measure the difference with `LENGTH`.

blocks.hint: `LENGTH('')` is `0`. `LENGTH(NULL)` is null, because the length of something unknown is also unknown. Dana Reyes and Owen Blake are invented contacts for this table, not people in the shipped data.

blocks.text: Row `1120` comes back with a length of `0`: there is a value, and it happens to be zero characters long. Row `1310` comes back with a null length, because a function given an unknown input can only produce an unknown answer. Nulls spread that way through almost every expression in SQL.
The column has to allow nulls

`CONTACT_NAME` in that table was declared `NOT NULL`. That is a rule stored in the table definition, and the engine enforces it on every write. Asking it to hold a null is not a warning; the statement is rejected and nothing changes.

-- This one fails on purpose. CONTACT_NAME was declared NOT NULL.
UPDATE CONTACT_LOG
SET CONTACT_NAME = NULL
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120';

-- SQLite reports: NOT NULL constraint failed: CONTACT_LOG.CONTACT_NAME
-- MySQL reports:  ERROR 1048 (23000): Column 'CONTACT_NAME' cannot be null

blocks.label: Why forbid nulls at all
blocks.text: Some columns are the reason the row exists. A contact with no name, an invoice with no number, a lease with no student: those rows cannot be used for anything. `NOT NULL` is how a designer says that out loud so no program can quietly break the rule later. Several columns in the course data are declared this way already, including `CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME`, `ITEM.DESCRIPTION`, and `STUDENT.LAST_NAME`. If a `SET column = NULL` is refused, the fix is almost never to remove the constraint. It is to ask whether that row should exist.
Finding the nulls afterward

Once a value is null, ordinary comparison stops working on it. `BALANCE = NULL` is not false, it is unknown, and a `WHERE` clause only keeps rows where the condition is definitely true. So the comparison matches nothing at all, including the very row you just emptied. `IS NULL` is the only test that works.

blocks.hint: Read `IS NULL` as a single operator, like `BETWEEN`. It is not the `=` sign with a different word after it.

blocks.label: The mirror image
blocks.text: `IS NOT NULL` keeps the rows that do have a value. `WHERE BALANCE IS NOT NULL` after the update above returns the other three customers, `1120`, `1225`, and `1420`. Together the two tests cover every row in the table, which plain `=` and `<>` never do once nulls are present.

items: Assign the bare keyword `NULL`, never the quoted text `'NULL'`
Include a `WHERE` clause, and test it as a `SELECT` first
Confirm the column is not declared `NOT NULL` before you try
Use null for unknown or not applicable, never as a stand-in for zero
Search for the result with `IS NULL`, never with `= NULL`
Expect `COUNT(column)`, `SUM`, and `AVG` to skip the nulled row

blocks.text: A table's structure is not carved in stone. Businesses change, and the tables have to follow. KimTay decides to email invoices instead of mailing them, so `CUSTOMER` needs somewhere to keep an email address. A supplier's product names outgrow the thirty characters `ITEM.DESCRIPTION` was given. A column nobody ever filled in is only creating confusion. All three are structure changes, and the statement that makes them is `ALTER TABLE`.
`ALTER TABLE` names the table, then states one change to it. Unlike `UPDATE`, it is not about rows: it changes what columns exist and what they are allowed to hold, for every row at once.
Adding a column

ALTER TABLE CUSTOMER
ADD COLUMN EMAIL VARCHAR(40);

The word `COLUMN` is optional in SQLite, in MySQL, and in Oracle, so `ADD EMAIL VARCHAR(40)` does the same job; Oracle also accepts a parenthesized list, `ADD (EMAIL VARCHAR2(40))`. Spelling out `ADD COLUMN` is the safer habit because it reads unambiguously everywhere. The new column always lands at the end of the table. `CUSTOMER` ships with nine columns ending in `REP_NUM`, so `EMAIL` becomes the tenth. No engine lets you insert a column in the middle.

blocks.starter:
-- Give CUSTOMER an EMAIL column, then record the address for
-- Access Pet Center (1120) and list all four customers with it.
blocks.hint: Two statements: one `ALTER TABLE` to create the column, one `UPDATE` to put a value in a single row.

blocks.label: Every existing row starts out null
blocks.text: The engine cannot invent email addresses for the four customers already stored, so it puts a null in each one. That is exactly the meaning you want here: the address is unknown, not blank. It also means the column you added in the morning will read as null all afternoon until somebody fills it in, and `COUNT(EMAIL)` will keep telling you how much of that work is left.
Because of that, you cannot add a `NOT NULL` column to a table that already has rows unless you also supply a `DEFAULT`. The engine would have to break the new rule the moment it created it.

-- Rejected: the engine would have to put null in five existing rows.
ALTER TABLE ITEM ADD COLUMN SUPPLIER VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL;

-- SQLite reports: Cannot add a NOT NULL column with default value NULL
-- Oracle reports ORA-01758: table must be empty to add mandatory (NOT NULL) column
Give it a default and the same statement succeeds, because now the engine has something legal to write into the rows that are already there.

blocks.starter:
-- Add a SUPPLIER column to ITEM that is required from now on.
-- Existing items have no supplier on file, so default them to 'UNKNOWN'.
blocks.hint: The clause order is type, then `NOT NULL`, then `DEFAULT`. All five items come back reading `UNKNOWN`.

blocks.text: Changing a column that is already there

Widening `CUSTOMER_NAME` from `VARCHAR(35)` to `VARCHAR(50)`, or changing `ON_HAND` from `SMALLINT` to `INTEGER`, is where the engines stop agreeing with each other. There is no portable statement. Learn the shape of the change, then look up the spelling for the engine in front of you.

blocks.caption: Changing an existing column, by engine
rows: `MODIFY` retypes; `CHANGE` renames and retypes at once
The parentheses around the column list are conventional
`ALTER TABLE CUSTOMER ALTER COLUMN CUSTOMER_NAME VARCHAR(50);`
Rebuild the table with the copy pattern below

blocks.label: Narrowing a column is a data change
blocks.text: Widening is safe. Going the other way is not: shortening `DESCRIPTION` to `VARCHAR(10)` has to do something with `Small Animal Grooming Kit`. Oracle refuses outright if any stored value is too long. MySQL in strict mode refuses as well, and outside strict mode it truncates the text and keeps going. Measure the longest value first with `SELECT MAX(LENGTH(DESCRIPTION)) FROM ITEM;` which reports `25` on the shipped data.

Renaming a column, without changing its type, is better supported: `ALTER TABLE REP RENAME COLUMN RATE TO COMMISSION_RATE;` works in MySQL 8.0, Oracle, and SQLite 3.25 and later, so it does run in the sandbox on this page. Every query, view, and report that spelled the old name breaks the instant you run it, so search your code for the old name first.
Removing a column

ALTER TABLE CUSTOMER
DROP COLUMN EMAIL;

blocks.starter:
-- Add EMAIL to CUSTOMER, look at the table, then take the column
-- back off and confirm CUSTOMER is shaped the way it started.
blocks.hint: The last `SELECT *` should come back with the original nine columns and no `EMAIL`.

blocks.label: Dropping a column takes its data with it
blocks.text: There is no undo and no recycle bin. If `EMAIL` held four hundred addresses, they are gone the moment the statement succeeds. Engines also refuse the request in several cases. `ALTER TABLE ITEM DROP COLUMN ITEM_ID;` fails with `cannot drop PRIMARY KEY column: "ITEM_ID"`, and dropping a column an index is built on fails too, with `error in index ... no such column`. Most engines block a column that is unique or pointed at by a foreign key until you remove that object first.
6-8a Making complex changes

Some changes have no single statement anywhere. Splitting one column into two. Reordering columns. Adding a primary key to a table that never had one. Turning a nullable column into `NOT NULL` after the fact. And, in SQLite, changing any column's type at all. For every one of these, the answer is the same four-step pattern, and it is worth learning even on engines that offer `MODIFY`, because it is the only approach that always works.

items.title: Create the replacement
items.body: `CREATE TABLE ITEM_NEW (...)` with the structure you actually want, under a temporary name. Write out every column, including the new or retyped ones, and carry over the constraints you are not deliberately changing. `ITEM.DESCRIPTION` is `VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL`, so the wider version stays `NOT NULL`.

items.title: Copy the rows across
items.body: `INSERT INTO ITEM_NEW (columns) SELECT columns FROM ITEM;` Name the columns on both sides. Any column in the new table that you leave out of the list stays null, which is what you want for a column that did not exist yesterday.

items.title: Check, then drop the original
items.body: Compare `COUNT(*)` on both tables and spot-check a row. Only then run `DROP TABLE ITEM;` This is the point of no return.

items.title: Rename the replacement
items.body: `ALTER TABLE ITEM_NEW RENAME TO ITEM;` Every query, view, and program that already refers to `ITEM` keeps working, because the name it asks for now points at the rebuilt table.

blocks.text: Here is the whole pattern on KimTay's `ITEM` table: `DESCRIPTION` gets wider, `ON_HAND` becomes a full `INTEGER`, and a `SUPPLIER` column appears. Everything else is copied over exactly as it was. Wrapping it in `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` matters, because step three destroys the original. If anything fails in between, the rollback leaves you with the table you started with instead of no table at all.

blocks.starter:
-- Rebuild ITEM so DESCRIPTION holds 40 characters, ON_HAND is an
-- INTEGER, and a SUPPLIER column exists. Leave CATEGORY, PRICE and
-- REORDER_LEVEL exactly as they are. Keep all five rows.
-- Use the four steps: create, copy, drop, rename.
blocks.hint: `SUPPLIER` is left out of the `INSERT` column list on purpose, so all five rows get a null there. Copying `CATEGORY` as `VARCHAR(15)` and `PRICE` as `DECIMAL(7,2)` keeps them unchanged; a rebuild is a chance to change things by accident as well as on purpose.

blocks.text: All five items survive, `SUPPLIER` is null on every row, and a join from `INVOICE_LINE` to `ITEM` still returns the same six lines it did before. Nothing outside the table had to change.

blocks.label: The copy carries rows, not rules
blocks.text: `DROP TABLE` takes the indexes, triggers, and views built on the old table with it, and any foreign key in another table that pointed at it is now aimed at a name that was briefly gone. Write the `CREATE INDEX` and `CREATE VIEW` statements you will need to run afterward before you start, and keep them in the same script. On a production database, take a backup first and rehearse the whole script on a copy.

items: `ADD COLUMN` puts the column last and fills existing rows with null
A `NOT NULL` column can only be added with a `DEFAULT`
Changing a column's type is MySQL `MODIFY`, Oracle `MODIFY (...)`, SQL Server `ALTER COLUMN`
SQLite cannot retype a column at all, so use the copy pattern
`DROP COLUMN` destroys the data in it and is refused on key or indexed columns
For anything else: create, copy, drop, rename, inside one transaction

blocks.text: `DROP TABLE` removes a table from the database. Not the rows in it, the table itself: the structure, the column definitions, the indexes, and every row inside. Afterward the name does not exist, and a query that mentions it fails the way a query for a misspelled table fails.
DROP TABLE ITEM_ARCHIVE;

That is the entire statement. Its brevity is the danger: there is no `WHERE`, no preview, and no confirmation prompt. Work through the whole life of a scratch table so you can see the before and the after.

Two supporting pieces show up in that walkthrough. `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` builds a brand-new table whose columns and rows both come from a query, which is the quickest way to make something disposable. And to ask the database which tables currently exist, SQLite reads its own catalog table, `sqlite_master`; MySQL answers the same question with `SHOW TABLES;` or `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES`. Module 7 covers catalogs properly, so treat this as a peek.

blocks.starter:
-- Build a scratch table holding the two Habitat items, list it,
-- confirm the database now has six tables, then drop it and
-- confirm the database is back to five.
blocks.hint: The archive should hold two rows, `AV07` and `FT88`. The first catalog list has six names; the second has five.

blocks.label: The rows go with the table
blocks.text: `DROP TABLE ITEM_ARCHIVE;` did not ask whether the two rows mattered. `DELETE FROM ITEM_ARCHIVE;` would have emptied the table and left the structure standing, ready to be refilled. `DROP TABLE` leaves nothing. On a real database, the only way back is a backup, so the question to answer before you press Enter is not whether you need the rows today but whether anyone needs them next quarter.
Dropping a table that might not be there

A setup script that starts by dropping yesterday's scratch tables fails on the very first run, because the tables do not exist yet. `IF EXISTS` turns that error into a no-op, which is why nearly every rebuild script is written this way.
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ITEM_ARCHIVE;

blocks.label: Engine support
blocks.text: `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` works in SQLite, MySQL, and SQL Server. Oracle had no `IF EXISTS` on `DROP TABLE` before 23ai; older Oracle scripts either accept the `ORA-00942: table or view does not exist` error or wrap the drop in a PL/SQL block that catches it. Note that `IF EXISTS` only suppresses the missing-table error. It does not suppress anything else, including a foreign key violation.
The foreign-key ordering problem

Tables are rarely alone. In KimTay's database `INVOICE_LINE` carries a foreign key to `ITEM` and another to `INVOICE`, and `INVOICE` carries one to `CUSTOMER`, which carries one to `REP`. Dropping `ITEM` while `INVOICE_LINE` still holds rows that name `AV07` leaves those rows pointing at a table that is gone. The lines still exist, but nothing can tell you what was ordered.

An engine that is enforcing foreign keys stops you. MySQL and Oracle do this by default; SQLite only does it when the check has been switched on for the session, which is why the sandbox on this page lets the drop through.

-- SQLite, with enforcement switched on for the session:
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
DROP TABLE ITEM;
-- Error: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed

-- MySQL says the same thing at more length:
-- ERROR 3730 (HY000): Cannot drop table 'ITEM' referenced by a
-- foreign key constraint on table 'invoice_line'.
The rule is to drop children before parents: a table that points at another table has to go first. Read the relationships backwards, from the most dependent table to the least.

items.title: List what points at what
items.body: In KimTay: `INVOICE_LINE` points at `INVOICE` and `ITEM`. `INVOICE` points at `CUSTOMER`. `CUSTOMER` points at `REP`. `ITEM` and `REP` point at nothing.

items.title: Drop the most dependent table first
items.body: `DROP TABLE INVOICE_LINE;` Nothing points at it, so it comes off cleanly.

items.title: Work outward
items.body: `DROP TABLE INVOICE;` then `DROP TABLE ITEM;` then `DROP TABLE CUSTOMER;` then `DROP TABLE REP;` Each one is safe because everything that referenced it is already gone. Only the dependencies are fixed, not the whole sequence: once `INVOICE_LINE` is gone, `INVOICE` and `ITEM` are independent of each other and may be dropped in either order.

items.title: Or remove the constraint instead
items.body: When you only want the one table gone, drop the foreign key from the child rather than the child itself: `ALTER TABLE INVOICE_LINE DROP FOREIGN KEY ...` in MySQL, `ALTER TABLE INVOICE_LINE DROP CONSTRAINT ...` in Oracle and SQL Server.

blocks.text: Now see the consequence for yourself. The sandbox on this page does not enforce foreign keys, so it will let you drop the parent, which makes it the perfect place to look at the wreckage.

Add `INNER JOIN ITEM` to that query and it does not return partial results, it fails outright with `no such table: ITEM`. Every report, view, and program that joined to `ITEM` broke at the same moment.

rows: The table, its columns, indexes, and other rows
An empty table you can insert into again
One column and its data (here, the column 6-8 added)
The table and all its other columns
The table, its rows, and its indexes

blocks.label: A habit worth keeping
blocks.text: Before dropping anything on a database that matters, run `CREATE TABLE ITEM_BACKUP AS SELECT * FROM ITEM;` first. It costs one statement and a little disk, and it turns an unrecoverable mistake into an inconvenient one. Note that the copy carries the rows only, not the primary key, the indexes, or the foreign keys, so it is a rescue kit rather than a replacement. Drop the backup when you are sure, which is usually a week later, not the same afternoon.

items: `DROP TABLE` removes the structure and every row, with no undo
`DELETE` empties a table; `DROP TABLE` erases it
Use `IF EXISTS` in scripts that may run more than once
Drop child tables before the parent tables they point at
Tables that do not reference each other may go in any order
Take a copy first: `CREATE TABLE X_BACKUP AS SELECT * FROM X;`

blocks.text: Module 6 moved you from asking a database questions to changing what it holds. The first half was about rows: creating a table, adding rows, correcting them, removing them, and doing that work inside a transaction so a half-finished change can be undone. The second half, sections 6-7 through 6-9, was about the shape of the tables themselves.

cards.title: Working with nulls
cards.body: `UPDATE ... SET column = NULL` empties a value on purpose, and it is the honest choice when a fact is unknown rather than zero. The column must not be declared `NOT NULL`. Find the result with `IS NULL`, never `= NULL`, and expect `COUNT(column)`, `SUM`, and `AVG` to skip the row.

cards.title: Reshaping a table
cards.body: `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` appends a column and nulls it on every existing row. `DROP COLUMN` destroys the column and its data. Changing a column's type is spelled differently in every engine and is not available in SQLite at all.

cards.title: Complex changes
cards.body: When no single statement will do it, create a new table with the structure you want, copy the rows in with `INSERT ... SELECT`, drop the original, and rename the replacement. Do it inside `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`, and plan to rebuild indexes and views.

cards.title: Removing tables
cards.body: `DROP TABLE` erases the structure and the rows together. `DELETE` only empties. Drop children before parents, or the foreign keys pointing at the parent will either block you or leave orphaned rows behind.

blocks.text: Underneath all four is one idea worth carrying into Module 7: statements that change data are not reversible by another query. A wrong `SELECT` wastes a minute. A wrong `UPDATE` without a `WHERE`, a wrong `DROP COLUMN`, or a wrong `DROP TABLE` costs whatever was in there. The professional habits are small and always the same: write the `SELECT` first, keep a backup or a transaction open, and change one thing at a time.

Several of those statements are MySQL and Oracle only. `GRANT` and `REVOKE` are not implemented in SQLite at all, and a view on this page can be created and queried but not updated through, so the text will name the engine each time.

blocks.label: Data definition versus data manipulation
blocks.text: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` change the rows inside a table and are called data manipulation, or DML. `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`, and `DROP TABLE` change what tables and columns exist and are called data definition, or DDL. The distinction matters on the job: in MySQL and Oracle, DDL commits your transaction the moment it runs, so a `ROLLBACK` after an `ALTER TABLE` will not put the column back. SQLite is the exception, which is why the rebuild pattern on this page can safely sit inside `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`.

One small check to keep the most confused pair straight. `IS NULL` is a test, and it returns `1` for true and `0` for false in this engine. Run it against a null, a zero, and an empty string at the same time.

blocks.starter:
-- Ask the engine directly: which of these three things is null?
SELECT NULL IS NULL AS null_is_null,
       0    IS NULL AS zero_is_null,
       ''   IS NULL AS empty_string_is_null;
blocks.hint: You should get `1`, `0`, `0`. Only the null is null; zero and the empty string are values.

blocks.text: The ten questions below are cumulative. Most of them are about sections 6-7 through 6-9, but several reach back to the `WHERE` clauses, joins, subqueries, and aggregate functions you have been using since Module 4, because that is how the material shows up in practice: a structure change is almost always followed by a query that has to still work. Read each scenario, decide before you look at the options, and read every note afterward, including the ones for the answers you did not pick.

blocks.label: How to use the notes
blocks.text: Each wrong option has a note naming the specific mistake it represents. Those mistakes are the ones that cost people real data, so the note is more valuable than the checkmark. If a note describes something you would have done, go back to the section it came from before moving on.

Before you start, warm up in the sandbox. This one combines a structure change from 6-8, a subquery from Module 5, and the null behavior from 6-7 in a single short script: KimTay wants to record, on each customer row, whether that customer was invoiced on June 14.

Downtown Aquarium & Pets was invoiced on the fifteenth, and Companion Care Clinic has never been invoiced at all, so both stay null. The counts confirm it: `4` customers, `2` with a known invoice date. Notice that you never had to write a null anywhere. `ADD COLUMN` supplied them, and the `WHERE` clause left them alone.

blocks.text: Six exercises, all of them on StayWell Student Accommodation except the last two, which return to KimTay. Work each one in the sandbox before opening the solution. Every sandbox on this page starts from a clean copy of the data, so a mistake costs you nothing except the time to reload.

blocks.label: Read the data first
blocks.text: StayWell has two properties, Millbrook Commons (`P100`) managed by Diane Ortiz and Sycamore Court (`P200`) managed by Bruce Feldman, five rooms between them, four students, four leases, and four payments. Check the column names before you type: rooms are described by `ROOM_TYPE`, `MONTHLY_RENT`, and `MAX_OCCUPANTS`, and a student's home state is `HOME_STATE`, not `STATE`. Every column in every row is filled in, which means any null you see after an exercise is one you or `ALTER TABLE` created.
Exercise 1: add a column and fill part of it

StayWell is putting up a page for each property. Give `PROPERTY` a `WEBSITE` column of forty characters, record `millbrookcommons.example` for Millbrook Commons, and list both properties. Sycamore Court has no page yet.

blocks.starter:
-- Add WEBSITE to PROPERTY, record the address for P100 only,
-- then list PROPERTY_ID, PROPERTY_NAME, and WEBSITE for both rows.
blocks.hint: You do not need a second `UPDATE` for Sycamore Court. `ADD COLUMN` already left it null, which is the correct value for a page that does not exist yet.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: set a value to null and watch the aggregates move

The studio at Sycamore Court, room `201`, is being converted and nobody has decided how many students it will hold. Set its `MAX_OCCUPANTS` to null, list the rooms whose capacity is unknown, then report how many rooms exist, how many have a known capacity, and how many occupants the five rooms now account for.

blocks.starter:
-- Null out MAX_OCCUPANTS for property P200 room 201, list the rooms
-- with an unknown capacity, then count rows, count capacities,
-- and sum the capacities.
blocks.solution:
UPDATE ROOM
SET MAX_OCCUPANTS = NULL
WHERE PROPERTY_ID = 'P200'
  AND ROOM_NUM = '201';

SELECT PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM, ROOM_TYPE, MAX_OCCUPANTS
FROM ROOM
WHERE MAX_OCCUPANTS IS NULL;

SELECT COUNT(*)             AS rooms,
       COUNT(MAX_OCCUPANTS) AS capacity_known,
       SUM(MAX_OCCUPANTS)   AS total_occupants
FROM ROOM;
blocks.hint: `ROOM` has a two-column primary key, so the `WHERE` clause needs both `PROPERTY_ID` and `ROOM_NUM` to reach exactly one row.

blocks.text: You should get `5` rooms, `4` with a known capacity, and `6` total occupants. Before the update the sum was `7`. The studio did not stop existing; the database stopped claiming to know how many people fit in it.
Exercise 3: null a value, then find the rows the wrong way

Layla Ibrahim's home state was entered from a form that has since been shown to be unreliable, so `HOME_STATE` for `S003` should be cleared. Do that, then write both `WHERE HOME_STATE = NULL` and `WHERE HOME_STATE IS NULL` and confirm which one finds her. Finish with a count of students and a count of known home states.

`ROOM_TYPE` is `VARCHAR(10)` today, too narrow for an entry like `Accessible Studio`. StayWell wants it widened to twenty characters, `MONTHLY_RENT` widened to `DECIMAL(9,2)`, and a new `NOTES` column of sixty characters. SQLite cannot retype a column, so rebuild the table. Keep all five rows, keep `MAX_OCCUPANTS` exactly as it is, and keep the two-column primary key. Wrap the whole thing in a transaction.

-- Rebuild ROOM: ROOM_TYPE VARCHAR(20), MONTHLY_RENT DECIMAL(9,2),
-- a new NOTES VARCHAR(60), primary key on (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM).
-- Create, copy, drop, rename. All five rooms must survive.

Back to KimTay. The bookkeeper wants a working copy of the invoice lines for June 14 so a pricing question can be checked without touching the real table. Build `LINE_REVIEW` from those lines, list it, then remove it completely and prove it is gone.

blocks.text: Exercise 6: order the drops correctly

KimTay is retiring the invoicing side of the database and keeping only `CUSTOMER` and `REP`. Write the `DROP TABLE` statements in an order that would not violate a single foreign key on an engine that enforces them, and confirm which tables are left. Use `IF EXISTS` so the script can be run twice.

-- Remove INVOICE_LINE, INVOICE, and ITEM in an order that would
-- satisfy an engine enforcing foreign keys. Then list what remains.
blocks.hint: `INVOICE_LINE` points at both of the others, so it has to go first. `INVOICE` and `ITEM` can then go in either order.

blocks.text: `CUSTOMER` and `REP` are what remain. Putting `INVOICE_LINE` anywhere but first would have failed on MySQL or Oracle, because it would still have held rows naming invoices or items that no longer existed, and `IF EXISTS` would not have rescued you: it suppresses a missing table, not a constraint violation. The sandbox does not enforce that check, which is exactly why the order is worth getting right by habit rather than by error message.

blocks.label: Before you do any of this for real
blocks.text: Every statement in these six exercises is permanent on a live database. On the job, the sequence is: write the `SELECT` that shows you the rows you are about to affect, take a backup or open a transaction, run one statement, check the result, and only then run the next. The sandbox forgives you. Production does not.

questions.stem: Companion Care Clinic, customer 1310, currently shows a BALANCE of 0.00. KimTay's bookkeeper learns the account was migrated from an older system and that nobody can confirm what the clinic actually owes. What should be stored in BALANCE, and why?
options: Leave it at 0.00, because the clinic has no invoices on file in the database
Store the text 'UNKNOWN' so a person reading the row understands the situation
Set it to null, because the amount is unknown rather than confirmed to be nothing
Set it to an empty string, which reads as blank and keeps the column numeric
optionNotes: Zero is a claim that the clinic owes nothing. Having no invoice yet is not the same as having a verified balance of zero.
BALANCE is a numeric column, so text will be rejected or coerced; and inventing a code word is what null exists to replace.
Correct: null means the value is unknown or does not apply, which is exactly the state of this balance.
An empty string is a text value of zero length, not an absence, and it does not belong in a DECIMAL column at all.
questions.takeaway: Null records that a fact is unknown; zero records that the fact is known and happens to be nothing.

questions.scenarioTitle: The average that moved on its own
questions.stem: A clerk at KimTay runs AVG(BALANCE) over the four customers and gets 2383.3125. She then sets Companion Care Clinic's balance to null and runs the identical query, which now returns 3177.75. SUM(BALANCE) reads 9533.25 both times. What happened?
options: AVG skipped the null row entirely, so the same total was divided by three instead of four
Setting a column to null adds the previous value into the next row's calculation
AVG treated the null as the highest balance in the table, which raised the average
The UPDATE removed the row from CUSTOMER, leaving three customers to average
optionNotes: Correct: aggregate functions ignore nulls. The row held 0.00, so the total was unchanged, but the divisor dropped from four to three.
Nulling a column never moves its old value anywhere. The value is gone.
Null has no magnitude at all, so it is neither the highest nor the lowest value; it is excluded from the calculation.
UPDATE changes a column in a row; it never deletes the row. COUNT(*) still returns 4.
questions.takeaway: COUNT(column), SUM, and AVG all skip nulls, so nulling one value changes the divisor as well as the total.

questions.stem: After nulling several balances, a KimTay analyst writes SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE = NULL; and gets back no rows at all, even though she can see nulls in the table. What is wrong?
options: The nulls were stored as the text 'NULL', so the comparison needs quotation marks around it
The query needs an ORDER BY clause before a WHERE clause can filter on a null column
BALANCE is numeric, and numeric columns require IS NOT DISTINCT FROM instead of equality
Nothing is ever equal to null, so the condition is never true and the WHERE keeps no rows
optionNotes: Nulls set with the bare keyword are not text. If they had been stored as the quoted string 'NULL' they would be findable by equality, which is one reason quoting the keyword is a bug rather than a shortcut.
ORDER BY only sorts the rows a WHERE clause has already kept; it has no effect on which rows match.
That operator exists in some engines but is not the lesson here, and equality fails on null in every column type, not only numeric ones.
Correct: comparing anything to null yields unknown, and a WHERE clause keeps only rows where the condition is definitely true.
questions.takeaway: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL are the only tests that work on nulls; = and <> silently match nothing.

questions.stem: A StayWell staff member tries UPDATE STUDENT SET LAST_NAME = NULL WHERE STUDENT_ID = 'S002'; and the engine rejects it with a NOT NULL constraint failure. The row is unchanged. What is the correct reading of this?
options: The database is out of space for the STUDENT table and must be rebuilt before updates work
LAST_NAME was defined as NOT NULL, so the designer decided a student row without a name is meaningless
Only columns in the primary key may be set to null, and LAST_NAME is not part of the key
The statement was missing a COMMIT, and adding one would let the null through
optionNotes: Constraint failures have nothing to do with disk space; the engine refused on a rule, not a resource.
Correct: STUDENT.LAST_NAME is declared NOT NULL in the table definition, and the engine enforces it on every write.
This is backwards. Primary key columns are the ones that must never be null; other columns are the ones that usually may be.
A rejected statement changed nothing, so there is nothing to commit. COMMIT never overrides a constraint.
questions.takeaway: A NOT NULL rejection is the table design working; the fix is to question the row, not to drop the constraint.

questions.stem: KimTay runs ALTER TABLE CUSTOMER ADD COLUMN EMAIL VARCHAR(40); on a table that already holds four customers. Immediately afterward, what does SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, EMAIL FROM CUSTOMER; return?
options: Four rows, with EMAIL null in every one of them, because the engine has no value to supply
Zero rows, because the existing rows do not yet match the new table structure
Four rows, with EMAIL holding an empty string, since text columns cannot hold nulls
An error, because a column cannot be added to a table that already contains data
optionNotes: Correct: ADD COLUMN appends the column and puts a null in it for every row that already exists.
Adding a column changes every row at once. No row is left behind or hidden.
CHAR and VARCHAR columns hold nulls perfectly well unless declared NOT NULL, and the engine does not substitute an empty string.
Adding a nullable column to a populated table is routine. Only a NOT NULL column without a DEFAULT is refused.
questions.takeaway: A newly added column is null on every existing row, which is why nulls and ALTER TABLE are taught together.

questions.stem: Product names have outgrown ITEM.DESCRIPTION, which is VARCHAR(30). The team needs VARCHAR(40). They are working in the SQLite engine behind this page. What has to happen?
options: Run ALTER TABLE ITEM MODIFY DESCRIPTION VARCHAR(40); which is the portable standard spelling
Delete every row, change the column, then reinsert the rows from a spreadsheet by hand
Rebuild the table: create ITEM_NEW with the wider column, copy the rows, drop ITEM, rename ITEM_NEW
Add a second column called DESCRIPTION_LONG and have every query read whichever one is filled
optionNotes: MODIFY is MySQL and Oracle syntax, and SQLite rejects it with 'near "MODIFY": syntax error'. There is no portable spelling for retyping a column.
Deleting the rows does not make the column wider, and retyping data by hand invites errors the copy pattern avoids entirely.
Correct: create, copy, drop, rename is the portable pattern and the only option in SQLite, which cannot retype a column.
Two columns holding the same fact is a design problem, and every query and report would then need to handle both.
questions.takeaway: When an engine will not change a column in place, rebuild the table under a new name and rename it into position.

questions.scenarioTitle: The rebuild that lost its index
questions.stem: A StayWell administrator rebuilds ROOM with the copy-and-rename pattern. All five rows arrive safely and every query returns correct results, but a nightly report that used to finish in seconds now takes minutes. What was most likely lost?
options: The primary key, which the pattern cannot recreate on a table with two key columns
An index that existed on the old ROOM table and was destroyed along with it by DROP TABLE
The MAX_OCCUPANTS values, which came across as nulls and forced the report to recompute them
The MONTHLY_RENT values, which came across as nulls and forced the report to recompute them
optionNotes: The primary key is part of the CREATE TABLE you write in step one, so it is recreated as long as you include it, and a two-column PRIMARY KEY clause is perfectly ordinary.
Correct: DROP TABLE removes the table's indexes with it, and the copy pattern carries rows, not the objects built on the table.
The results are correct, so the values arrived intact. Nulled capacities would have produced wrong numbers, not slow ones.
Same problem: a null rent would change the report's output, and the scenario says the output is right and only the speed changed.
questions.takeaway: The copy pattern moves rows only; plan to recreate indexes, views, and triggers in the same script.

questions.scenarioTitle: Two ways to clear the archive
questions.stem: KimTay keeps a scratch table, ITEM_ARCHIVE, that a Monday-morning script refills with INSERT statements. The script assumes the table is already there and never creates it. On Friday the team wants the table emptied, but wants Monday's script to keep working without any change. Which statement fits?
options: DROP TABLE ITEM_ARCHIVE; because dropping is always cleaner than emptying
ALTER TABLE ITEM_ARCHIVE DROP COLUMN ITEM_ID; to remove the rows through the key column
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ITEM_ARCHIVE; which removes the rows but preserves the column definitions
DELETE FROM ITEM_ARCHIVE; because it removes every row and leaves the table ready to refill
optionNotes: This erases the structure too, so Monday's insert-only script would fail with 'no such table' instead of filling the table.
Dropping a column removes one column from every row; it does not remove rows, and where the column is a key or is indexed the engine refuses outright.
IF EXISTS only prevents an error when the table is absent. The statement still destroys the structure along with the rows, so Monday's script still fails.
Correct: DELETE empties the table and leaves its structure standing, so an insert-only script keeps working unchanged.
questions.takeaway: DELETE empties a table; DROP TABLE erases it, structure and all.

questions.scenarioTitle: Retiring the invoice tables at KimTay
questions.stem: KimTay is removing INVOICE_LINE, INVOICE, and ITEM from a MySQL database that enforces foreign keys. INVOICE_LINE references both INVOICE and ITEM, and neither INVOICE nor ITEM references the other. In what order must the drops run?
options: ITEM, then INVOICE, then INVOICE_LINE, working from the smallest table to the largest
INVOICE, then ITEM, then INVOICE_LINE, because invoices are the subject of the other two
INVOICE_LINE, then INVOICE and ITEM in either order, because the child must go first
Any order at all, since MySQL reorders drop statements automatically to satisfy constraints
optionNotes: Row counts are irrelevant. Dropping ITEM first is refused, because INVOICE_LINE still holds rows referencing it.
This drops a parent before its child as well, so the first statement fails on the constraint from INVOICE_LINE.
Correct: the table holding the foreign keys goes first, after which nothing references INVOICE or ITEM and the two remaining drops are independent of each other.
No engine reorders your statements. Each DROP is evaluated on its own and fails if a constraint still points at the table.
questions.takeaway: Drop children before parents; tables that do not reference each other may go in any order.

questions.stem: Someone drops ITEM on a KimTay database that is not enforcing foreign keys. All six INVOICE_LINE rows are still present. A report then runs SELECT L.INVOICE_NUM, I.DESCRIPTION FROM INVOICE_LINE L INNER JOIN ITEM I ON L.ITEM_ID = I.ITEM_ID; What happens, and what is the underlying problem?
options: The query fails with no such table ITEM, and the surviving lines now reference a table that is gone
The query returns the six lines with DESCRIPTION shown as null, since the join finds no match
The query returns nothing but succeeds, because an inner join with a missing table yields an empty result
The query returns the six lines unchanged, because INVOICE_LINE already stores its own description text
optionNotes: Correct: the engine cannot resolve the table name at all, so the statement fails outright, and the invoice lines are orphaned.
That is what an outer join to an existing but unmatched table would do. A missing table is a different failure entirely.
A missing table is caught when the statement is prepared, not an empty result set. The query never runs.
INVOICE_LINE stores ITEM_ID, NUM_ORDERED, and QUOTED_PRICE only. The description lived exclusively in ITEM.
questions.takeaway: Dropping a parent table does not clean up the rows that referenced it; it leaves orphans and breaks every query that joined to it.

matchers.heading: Sort the Module 6 Statements
matchers.prompt: Each card describes one thing a database professional did this week. Drop it into the part of Module 6 it belongs to. Every card fits exactly one zone.

cards.text: Clearing Companion Care Clinic's BALANCE because the migrated amount cannot be confirmed
cards.why: Assigning the NULL keyword with UPDATE is how you record that a value is unknown.

cards.text: Rewriting WHERE BALANCE = NULL as WHERE BALANCE IS NULL so the query finds the row
cards.why: IS NULL is the only comparison that matches an absent value.

cards.text: Giving CUSTOMER an EMAIL column so invoices can be sent electronically
cards.why: ADD COLUMN appends one column to an existing table in a single statement.

cards.text: Removing a column nobody ever filled in, and its data along with it
cards.why: DROP COLUMN is a single ALTER TABLE change that destroys that column's data.

cards.text: Widening ITEM.DESCRIPTION from thirty to forty characters while working in SQLite
cards.why: SQLite cannot retype a column, so the table has to be rebuilt under a new name.

cards.text: Copying every row into a replacement table, then renaming it back over the original
cards.why: Create, copy, drop, rename is the four-step pattern for any change no statement supports.

cards.text: Erasing the ITEM_ARCHIVE scratch table and every row inside it in one statement
cards.why: DROP TABLE removes the structure and the rows together, with no undo.

cards.text: Removing INVOICE_LINE before INVOICE so no foreign key is left pointing at nothing
cards.why: Child tables must be dropped before the parent tables their foreign keys reference.
